blocks.text: Varro also reports that the ancients used (salt) as a relish: for they ate salt with bread and cheese, as the proverb shows. So Pliny, book 31, ch. 7, where shortly before the same author says: It is also involved in honours and in military service: hence salaries are so called, with great authority among the ancients. Likewise, Ancus Martius, the king, gave the people six thousand modii of salt as a largess. The kings of Assyria also gave salt as pay. Accordingly, in Esdr. IV, 14. the governors of Samaria write this to King Artaxerxes: Because די־מלח היכלא מלחנא, we are salted with the salt of the palace. That is the literal rendering; that is, as Junius rightly puts it, we receive a salary from the king's palace. But no one praises salt more fully than Plutarch, Sympos. book 5, Probl. 10, where, on the question why Homer ^{a)} calls salt divine, he asserts among other things that salt is τῶν ἄλλων ὄψων ὄψον εἶναι, καὶ ἥδυσμα [tōn allōn opsōn opson einai, kai hēdysma], the relish and seasoning of all other relishes. Likewise, Θρίγκωμα τῆς τροφῆς γινόμενον εἰς τὸ σῶμα, καὶ παρέχον ἐναρμοσίαν αὐτῇ προς τὴν ὄρεξιν [thrinkōma tēs trophēs ginomenon eis to sōma, kai parechon enarmosian autē pros tēn orexin], that which becomes a safeguard of food in the body, making it agreeable and suited to our palate. Hence in Sirach. XXXIX, 31. certain things are praised as [II, 576] ἀρχὴ πάσης χρείας εἰς ζωὴν ἀνθρώπου [archē pasēs chreias eis zōēn anthrōpou], the beginning (that is, the chief) of all things necessary for life. And among these salt comes before all food. But whatever may be said of salt, this much is certain: salt is nothing but [col. 41] a seasoning, and seasonings are not usually bought at a great price in a severe famine, when food is lacking. For hunger itself is the best seasoning, and one does not then seek what stimulates the palate, but what satisfies.

V. The fifth opinion is that of the Talmudists. To understand it, the reader must first be told that there is this Talmudic axiom in the tractate Megilla, ch. 3: כל המקראות הכתובין בתורה לגנאי קורין אותן לשבח, All words written indecently in the Law are read decently. Therefore, wherever words occur in Scripture that are less decent in common usage, the teachers of the Hebrews, out of regard for decency, wanted them read otherwise than they are written. So in place of the word found in the text they substitute in the margin another, more decent one, which it is still the custom today to read in its place in the synagogues. Hence for שגל^{b)}, to have intercourse, they read שכב, to lie with; for עפולים^{c)}, diseases of the anus, טחורים, haemorrhoids; for טחוראות^{d)}, latrines, properly places of dung, מוצאות, privies; for חורים and שינים^{e)}, dung and urine, צואה and מימי רגלים, excrement and water of the feet. In the same way, in this passage, for חריונים, dove's dung, they want דביונים to be read, the flux of doves, a word compounded of דב, flux, and יונים, doves. But the Talmudists interpret דביונים differently, as if it were compounded of the Chaldee pronoun ד, which corresponds to the Hebrew אשר, who, which, that, the preposition ב, in, and the noun יונים, doves. For them, then, דביונים means that which (supply: is or was) in the doves. For they hold that at Samaria doves had been trained to go out foraging in the fields, so to speak; and that when they returned stuffed and swollen, their owners shook out their crops, extracted the grain and sold it at a high price. So, in their view, the words of the sacred text run thus: The famine in Samaria was so great that a quarter of a kab of the grains that were in the doves, and were extracted from their crops, sold for five shekels. Hence Comestor in the Historia Scholastica, book 4 of Kings, ch. 10: Some relate that by the word dung is meant the little bladder of the dove, in which were found grains brought from outside. I do not think anything more absurd than this fiction could have been devised. Not that I deny that doves, through love of their young, can be so trained that, released from a besieged city, they return home; for we have shown in the immediately preceding chapter that ancient and more recent people often used such messengers. But who would believe that at Samaria there were so many such docile doves? Or that in fields laid waste far and wide by the enemy they found crops everywhere at hand? Or that, returning with full crops, [II, 577] they so easily disgorged whatever they had swallowed in the field? And that by such arts even one kab of grain could have been gathered in the whole time of the siege? Or, if God had sustained this people for some time in so miraculous a way, that Scripture would have passed over so unheard-of a thing so lightly? But we argue in vain, since the word חריונים, which is in the text, can in no way be drawn to this sense. Indeed, hardly, or not even hardly, can the marginal word דביונים be rendered that which is in the doves, unless we suppose that a Chaldee pronoun was prefixed to a Hebrew noun, and so a hybrid, half-barbarous word was formed.
